04 · Read & review

The transcript

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

Fiona Bell's latest message contained a second extract from the trust's 2011 accounting guidance. Emma opened it beside her notes on the words “manual approval”, which had appeared in the preliminary records without any confirmed signatory or linked transfer.

The guidance described a two-stage arrangement. A member of staff could request an exceptional payment decision; a person with delegated authority was then supposed to authorise it. Both actions should be recorded, together with dates and reference numbers. The passage supplied roles, not individual names, and did not establish that the procedure had been followed in every case.

“So it required two signatures?” Sarah asked.

“Not necessarily signatures,” Emma replied. “The document says the request and authorisation should be recorded separately. We still need to see how that happened.”

When Emma spoke to Fiona, she asked whether the team had identified actual authorisers. Fiona said they had not. Several entries apparently bore a manual-approval notation, but adjacent fields were unclear on the surviving copies. Staff were preparing better images before attempting a reliable count or matching the entries to later transactions.

Emma resisted interpreting illegible fields as missing signatures. A poor copy was not evidence that the original record had been left blank. Equally, the existence of a policy did not verify compliance.

She turned back to Helen Ward's redacted letter. Its selection decision was conditional on further checks, and the family had not established that a grant was ultimately paid. Nothing linked that application to the exceptional-payment material. Helen subsequently confirmed that her cousin was happy for general questions about procedure to be asked but did not wish to disclose further banking information. Emma accepted the boundary.

By afternoon, her notebook contained four headings: Requested, Authorised, Transferred and Received. A payment request might never be approved; an authorisation might not lead to a transfer; a transfer might be returned. She could not collapse any of the stages into another.

Fiona's final email introduced a further lead. The inventory included a sheet labelled “Delegated authority — September 2011”, but its contents had not been examined. It might explain who was entitled to approve exceptions, though it could just as easily list positions rather than named individuals.

Sarah remembered the anonymous caller's advice to ask who approved payments. Emma remembered it too, without assuming the caller was trustworthy. The new title made the question investigable; it did not answer it.

She asked Fiona for a non-identifying description of the sheet once it had been examined. Until then, the strongest finding was a procedural distinction, not a scandal.
